title: Measurements and Significant Figures
short: Read an instrument to one estimated digit, then count the digits that carry meaning.
trouble: Students count leading zeros as significant, drop a meaningful trailing zero such as the one in 2.50 g, or report only the digits that have tick marks.

blocks.html: Every measurement has some uncertainty. A ruler marked every millimeter cannot tell you a length to the nearest thousandth of a millimeter. Scientists show how exact a measurement is by how many digits they write. You already know Rounding Decimals; significant figures tell you where to round.

Record all the digits you are sure of plus one estimated digit. Those are the significant figures. Nonzero digits always count; zeros between them count; leading zeros never count; trailing zeros count when there is a decimal point.

Digits carry information about the measurement. In $0.0045\ \text{m}$, the zeros only place the decimal point: the same length is $4.5\ \text{mm}$, with no zeros at all, so they cannot be significant. In $2.50\ \text{g}$, the final 0 says the balance read the hundredths place and found 0 there, which is real information: writing $2.5\ \text{g}$ would claim less.

blocks.title: Counting
blocks.q: How many significant figures are in $0.004050\ \text{L}$?
steps: Start at the first nonzero digit, the 4. The three zeros before it don't count.
The final 0 comes after a decimal point, so it counts too.

blocks.title: Rounding to three
steps: The first three significant digits are 3, 4 and 5.
The next digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so round the 5 up to 6.
Keep the leading zeros to hold the place value.

blocks.html: Counting leading zeros ($0.0062$ has 2 significant figures, not 5), dropping a meaningful trailing zero (writing 2.5 g when the balance read 2.50 g), or recording only the digits that have tick marks. Check by rewriting the number in scientific notation: $0.0062 = 6.2 \times 10^{-3}$ shows 2 digits.
